item.title: Stable Baselines3 declared stable with focus on maintenance
item.description:
Stable Baselines3 declared stable with focus on maintenance

Stable Baselines3 (SB3) has reached a stable state as most features from the original roadmap have been implemented. Development focus has shifted to bug fixes and maintenance, including documentation updates and user experience improvements, while newer algorithms continue to be developed in associated repositories.

🔍 Overview

Stable Baselines3 is a set of reliable implementations of reinforcement learning algorithms in PyTorch. It is the next major version of Stable Baselines. The toolset is designed to be simple for beginners to experiment with advanced RL concepts without being buried in implementation details, though it assumes some prior knowledge about Reinforcement Learning.

🧩 How it works

The algorithms are intended to make it easier for the research community and industry to replicate, refine, and identify new ideas. They serve as baselines to build projects on top of and as a tool for comparing new approaches against existing ones. The performance of each algorithm was tested, and detailed logs and reports are provided on the OpenRL Benchmark platform.

⚙️ Key details

  • Core Library: SB3 provides reliable PyTorch implementations of RL algorithms.
  • Associated Repositories:
    • SB3 Contrib: Newer algorithms are regularly added here.
    • SBX: Faster variants are developed in this SB3 + Jax repository.
    • RL Zoo: An active training framework with its own roadmap.
  • Integrations: SB3 includes integrations with Weights & Biases for experiment tracking and Hugging Face for storing and sharing trained models.
  • Migration: A migration guide from SB2 to SB3 is available in the documentation.

🚀 Availability

Documentation is available online at https://stable-baselines3.readthedocs.io/. Detailed presentations of SB3 can be found in the v1.0 blog post or the associated JMLR paper. RL Baselines3 Zoo, part of the ecosystem, provides scripts for training, evaluating agents, tuning hyperparameters, plotting results, and recording videos. It also includes a collection of tuned hyperparameters for common environments and RL algorithms, along with agents trained with those settings, providing a simple interface to train and enjoy RL agents and benchmark different algorithms.

item.title: VAGEN framework introduced for training multi-turn vision-language model agents
item.description:
VAGEN framework introduced for training multi-turn vision-language model agents

VAGEN is a new reinforcement learning (RL) framework specifically designed for training multi-turn vision-language model (VLM) agents. The framework enables these agents to build an internal world model through explicit visual state reasoning.

🔍 Overview

  • VAGEN functions as a multi-turn reinforcement learning framework built for VLM agents.
  • It supports a novel approach called World Modeling RL, which improves multi-turn performance by explicitly supervising the world model reasoning process.
  • The framework frames multi-turn VLM agentic tasks as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP).

🧩 How it works

  • World Modeling RL: A reinforcement learning approach that supervises the world model reasoning process to enhance agent performance.
  • StateEstimation: A reinforcement signal that helps the agent determine “what is the current state?”
  • TransitionModeling: A reinforcement signal that helps the agent determine “what comes next?”
  • LLM-as-Judge: Used to provide a world-modeling reward for the StateEstimation and TransitionModeling signals.
  • Architecture Decoupling: The reusable harness, environment, model, rollout, and evaluation boundaries keep world-modeling signals independent from the selected training algorithm.

⚙️ Key details

  • VAGEN-Lite: A lightweight and clean reimplementation of VAGEN built on the VERL agent-loop for easy customization and stable performance.
  • Version Support: Added support for Verl 0.9.0, which decoupled the environment and harness layer.
  • Legacy Code: Previous full-featured releases are available on the vagen-legacy branch, and the last commit before major updates is tagged as vagen-lite-verl-v0.6.1-final.

🚀 Availability

  • VAGEN-Lite Release: Introducing VAGEN-Lite in December 2025 as a lightweight reimplementation.
  • Branch Migration: The main branch migrated to VAGEN-Lite in February 2026.
  • Verl Update: Support for Verl 0.9.0 added in August 2026, marking a major update that decoupled the environment and harness layer.

item.title: Laminar Enables Scalable Asynchronous RL Post-Training for LLMs
item.description:
Laminar Enables Scalable Asynchronous RL Post-Training for LLMs

Laminar is a scalable reinforcement learning post‑training framework that enables large language models and long‑horizon agents to be fine‑tuned at scale.

🔍 Overview

  • Built on verl and Uni-Agent.
  • Open‑source implementation of Laminar: A Scalable Asynchronous RL Post‑Training Framework (EuroSys ’26).
  • Decoupled, asynchronous, and fault‑tolerant design for large‑cluster scaling.

🧩 How it Works

  • Fully decoupled training and rollout: independent loops via data and weight planes.
  • Data plane (ExperienceBuffer) buffers completed trajectories for AsyncRLTrainer.
  • Weight plane (Relay) stages published weights for inference replicas to pull on demand.
  • Trajectory‑level asynchrony: generates and consumes individual trajectories independently.
  • Version‑mixed partial rollout: interrupts in‑flight generations on weight sync and continues with newer weights.
  • Version‑consistent rollout: keeps each trajectory on a single model version.
  • Dynamic repack: consolidates long‑tail trajectories onto fewer replicas, freeing drained replicas to pull the latest weights.
  • Concurrent multi‑checkpoint evaluation (laminar.eval): version‑pinned routing and tail repacking for bubble‑free offline batch and online streaming evaluation.
  • Fault‑tolerant execution: prevents single‑replica failures from stalling cluster‑wide progress.
  • Inference engines recover failed replicas from Relay or checkpoint storage while preserving in‑flight trajectory prefixes.
  • Trainer engine resumes from the latest checkpoint (asynchronous per‑step checkpoint in progress).

⚙️ Key Details

  • Extras
1
2
3
4

--extra vllm vLLM rollout and evaluation backend
--extra megatron Megatron‑LM training backend
--extra fsdp FSDP2 training backend
--extra ucx UCX transport for Relay (recommended)

🚀 Availability

  • Open‑source on GitHub (built on verl and Uni-Agent).
  • Manages Python, CUDA, wheel indexes, and pinned Git dependencies with uv (see pyproject.toml and uv.lock).

💡 Why it Matters

  • In SWE agent training (Qwen3‑Coder‑30B‑A3B‑Instruct on SWE‑rebench, evaluated on SWE‑bench Verified on 64×H800) it improved resolve rate from 46.6 % to 52.2 %, surpassing the baseline peak of 51.4 %.
  • Uses 33 % fewer trained samples and 64 % fewer GPU‑hours to exceed the baseline peak.

item.title: New Deployment Method Bridges Real Vehicle Gap for Autonomous Driving Models
item.description:
New Deployment Method Bridges Real Vehicle Gap for Autonomous Driving Models

Intro

A new deployment methodology called Released-to-Real (R2R) addresses the gap between high-performing autonomous-driving models and their real-world vehicle deployment. The approach corrects source-system coupling while improving success rates and sensor accuracy.

🔍 Overview

The research identifies why released autonomous-driving models struggle when deployed on new real vehicles. Even after conventional adaptation, these models remain coupled to assumptions from their source sensing, data, and execution processes.

🧩 How it works

R2R Methodology

  • Identifies source-system coupling in released models
  • Corrects only affected components while preserving the original model
  • Achieves sensor adaptation across multiple released detectors and three real sensor rigs

Human-Anchored Reinforcement Learning (HA-RL)

  • Corrects trajectory-level optimization mismatch through recorded target driving data
  • Avoids costly rollouts of generative closed-loop reinforcement learning
  • Operates on the ego state rather than observation inputs

Sensor Adaptation

  • Localizes and corrects source-dependent spatial and temporal representations
  • Uses frozen perception weights
  • Requires neither target annotations nor retraining

⚙️ Key Details

Component Description
HA-RL Corrects ego state mismatch for data and behavior adaptation
Sensor Adaptation Handles physical sensor adaptation with frozen weights
Multi-Camera Support Improves multi-camera detector performance on target rigs

item.title: New robotics research addresses VLA brittleness with neuro-symbolic integration
item.description:
New robotics research addresses VLA brittleness with neuro-symbolic integration

Several new robotics papers submitted on 23 Nov 2026 address persistent barriers in real-world robot deployment, focusing on reliability, safety auditing, and robustness under coupled uncertainties.

🧩 Proposed Frameworks

Researchers have introduced multiple methodologies to overcome the limitations of current end-to-end systems, such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, which often exhibit brittle generalization and inconsistent motor control under distribution shifts.

  • Embodied Neuro-Symbolic (NeSy) AI: A deployment-oriented paradigm that integrates learned perception, planning, and control with explicit, machine-readable background knowledge and formal constraints.
  • Collision Rendering: The first trajectory planning framework on sparse voxel radiance fields (SVR), supporting GPU-accelerated, risk-bounded collision checking and differentiable collision cost.
  • Co-DRIS + SuperMimic: A perception-action co-design framework for reactive robotic manipulation that couples an inertial world-frame physics-informed world model with an action-conditioned dual-stream causal GRU belief encoder.
  • RESET: A framework that reconstructs contact-rich worlds from a single real demonstration to enable self-improvement of robot manipulation skills without runtime LLM calls.

⚙️ Key Technical Details

  • Collision Rendering: Approximates robots with collision spheres and uses a probabilistic collision model to derive upper bounds on directional collision probability via a GPU-accelerated rendering pipeline. It integrates with sampling-based planners without auxiliary geometric maps.
  • Co-DRIS + SuperMimic: Addresses the degradation seen in single-frame frameworks (like DRIS) when perception and actuation uncertainties co-occur. It includes phase-aware variable-impedance soft-catching that transitions a 7-DoF Franka Research 3 arm into an overdamped regime.
  • RESET: Uses open-loop replay and silhouette consistency to examine reconstructed worlds, evolving modular white-box task graphs from per-node failure evidence. It allows skills to be shared with unseen robots without new demonstrations.

📊 Performance and Results

Framework Context Performance
DRIS Isolated uncertainties 86.4%
DRIS Coupled stress scenarios 27.6%
Co-DRIS + SuperMimic Coupled/dropout stress scenarios 66.6%
Co-DRIS + SuperMimic 4-sigma noise 70.5%
RESET Average success on unseen layouts 97%
RESET Real-robot trials 80% success in 280 trials
RESET Cross-robot skill copying 95% of skill functions unchanged

💡 Why it matters

Current VLA pipelines offer limited ways to express and audit safety constraints, making assurance difficult in safety-critical settings. The proposed Embodied NeSy AI supports scalable, trustworthy robot deployment by enabling auditable, machine-checkable compliance with safety and operational requirements. Additionally, these new frameworks aim to bridge the gap between simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks, where ground-truth success scorers and resettable environments are typically unavailable.

#Robotics #NeuroSymbolicAI #TrajectoryPlanning #ReinforcementLearning #CollisionDetection

item.title: FineEnvs: An Open-Source Resource for End-to-End RL Environments
item.description:
FineEnvs: An Open-Source Resource for End-to-End RL Environments

A new open-source resource called FineEnvs has been released to address the shifting bottleneck in reinforcement learning (RL) for LLMs, where the environment design now poses a greater challenge than the algorithm. The project provides an end-to-end, reproducible, and open-source framework for designing, building, deploying, training against, and scaling RL environments to thousands of concurrent sessions.

🧩 How it works

The ecosystem is built on real, executable code rather than diagrams or unverified examples. Key characteristics of the resource include:

  • Reproducible Training: Every rollout has been executed, and every training curve comes from a job that users can launch in a single command without requiring their own GPU.
  • Comprehensive Coverage: The resource covers how to design an environment, how to build it, how to deploy it, how to train against it, and how to scale it to thousands of concurrent sessions.
  • Framework Agnosticism: The environments are compatible with six different frameworks, allowing users to train using SETA, native OpenCode, or Harbor, utilizing HF Jobs or Slurm.
  • Verified SFT Traces: Includes data-analysis tasks with verified SFT traces and a single-turn GRPO tutorial on HF Jobs.

⚙️ Key details

The release features three distinct environments demonstrated across six frameworks side by side. These environments utilize specific models and reward mechanisms:

Environment / Task Description Model / Reward Mechanism
Math Image OCR Train models to read math images into LaTeX Qwen3-VL-2B with a verifiable reward
Watercolour Painting Train models to paint watercolours by writing p5.brush sketches Qwen3.5-35B-A3B rewarded by an aesthetic preference model
VLM Navigation Drop a VLM at a random street corner on Earth Scored on kilometres of error
Document OCR & ASR OCR over a million pages in 22 languages and speech recognition over 102 Behind one OpenEnv server; Gemma 4 trained to read and hear Kannada

🚀 Availability

The resource is accessible through the following locations:

  • Source, recipes, and notebooks: Available in the project repository.
  • Environments, datasets, models, and demos: Hosted at huggingface.co/FineEnvs.
  • Training Infrastructure: Supports execution via HF Jobs or Slurm.

item.title: Gymnasium-Robotics Library Releases with Reinforcement Learning Robotic Environments
item.description:
Gymnasium-Robotics Library Releases with Reinforcement Learning Robotic Environments

The Gymnasium-Robotics library has been released, offering a collection of Reinforcement Learning robotic environments built on the Gymnasium API and powered by the MuJoCo physics engine. Users can install environments via pip, with support for both the maintained MuJoCo Python bindings and legacy mujoco-py versions through optional extras. The package is officially supported on Linux and macOS, with community contributions welcomed for Windows compatibility.

🧩 Available Environments

  • Fetch Environments: 7-degree-of-freedom robot arm for tasks including Reach, Push, Slide, and Pick and Place
  • Shadow Dexterous Hand Environments: 24-degree-of-freedom anthropomorphic hand for object manipulation with cube, egg-object, or pen
  • Maze Environments: Navigation tasks using 2-DoF force-controlled ball or Ant agent, with varying maze complexity
  • Adroit Arm Environments: Shadow Dexterous Hand with additional arm degrees of freedom for hammering, door opening, pen twirling, and ball manipulation
  • Franka Kitchen Environments: 9-DoF Franka robot arm in a kitchen setting for multitask interaction scenarios
  • MaMuJoCo: Multi-agent factorizations using pettingzoo.ParallelEnv API
  • D4RL Environments: Now available with refactored action/observation spaces

⚙️ API and Features

The environments extend the core Gymnasium API by inheriting from GoalEnv class, which enforces:

  • Dictionary observation space containing three required keys
  • Exposed reward, terminated, and truncated signals for flexible goal re-computation
  • Compatibility with Hindsight Experience Replay (HER) algorithms

Some environment variations include data from 92 touch sensors in the observation space.

item.title: gym-pybullet-drones refactored for gymnasium and Betaflight SITL
item.description:
gym-pybullet-drones refactored for gymnasium and Betaflight SITL

A minimalist refactoring of the gym-pybullet-drones repository has been released to ensure compatibility with gymnasium, stable-baselines3 2.0, and betaflight SIM. The project, originally featured in GitHub’s Maintainer Spotlight 2026, now supports both single-agent and multi-agent tasks with updated system requirements.

🔍 Overview

  • Refactoring Goal: Minimalist update for compatibility with gymnasium, stable-baselines3 2.0, and betaflight SITL.
  • Version Control: The original IROS 2021 codebase is accessible via git checkout [paper|master].
  • Citation: Users are encouraged to cite the IROS 2021 paper and the original codebase.

🧩 How it works

  • Single-Agent Task: One drone hovers at z == 1.0.
  • Multi-Agent Task: Two drones hover at z == 1.2 and 0.7 respectively.
  • PettingZooWrapper: Exposes multi-drone aviary through PettingZoo’s Parallel API, assigning one agent per drone (drone_0, drone_1, …).
  • Observation and Reward: Each agent receives its own row of the aviary’s observation. The aviary’s team reward and episode flags are shared by all agents.
  • Centralized Critics: env.state() returns every drone’s kinematics for centralized critics.

⚙️ Key details

Requirement Details
Operating Systems Tested on Intel x64/Ubuntu 24.04 and Apple Silicon/macOS 26
Python & pybullet Requires Python 3.10+; pybullet has no pre-built wheel for versions beyond 3.10
Ubuntu Setup Install gcc to allow pip3 install to build pybullet
SITL Setup One-time setup requires building one SITL executable per drone from the repo’s top folder
Dependencies --num_drones must be less than or equal to the number passed to clone_bfs.sh; curl may be required via apt install

💡 Why it matters

The PettingZooWrapper makes the environment usable with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) libraries built on PettingZoo. The refactoring ensures the environment remains functional with modern reinforcement learning stacks like stable-baselines3 2.0 while supporting Betaflight SITL for drone simulation.

item.title: Hugging Face introduces RL-trained harness adapters for improved LLM efficiency
item.description:
Hugging Face introduces RL-trained harness adapters for improved LLM efficiency

Hugging Face has introduced “harness adapters,” a method for adapting favorite models to specific agent harnesses using reinforcement learning (RL) to improve performance and cost efficiency. While base models generally target general performance, combining a model with a specific harness often leaves performance and efficiency on the table for targeted tasks. By training custom adapters on specific task distributions, developers can squeeze more capability out of existing models for their specific use cases.

🧩 How it works

The technique involves combining RL on a custom task distribution with the user’s favorite agent harness. This process yields more accurate and efficient models specifically for that target harness and task combination. The core mechanism is that models are not fully optimized for every harness and task; they are optimized for general performance. With RL, a custom harness adapter can be trained to optimize the model for the specific harness and task at hand.

In recent experiments, researchers froze the weights of the Qwen3.8-27B model and added a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter. This approach resulted in the model reasoning less, calling fewer tools, and performing better on the first attempt.

Model / Configuration Terminal-Bench 2.1 Score Avg Tokens per Task
Qwen3.8-27B (Base) 39% 2.9K
Qwen3.8-27B (with RL LoRA) 55% 1.5K

⚙️ Key details

To validate this approach on harder real-world software engineering tasks, the team trained one LoRA adapter for Qwen3.8-27B for each of three agent harnesses: Pi, Hermes Agent, and OpenCode. The RL training occurred inside the harness itself. Datasets, training, and agent rollouts were managed on the Hub in Jobs using TRL’s AsyncGRPOTrainer, OpenEnv, and harbor.

Key technical components of the recipe include:

  • Super Adapter: The three individual LoRAs were merged into a single “super adapter” that runs unchanged under all three harnesses.
  • Docker Images: Ready-to-use docker images for RL tasks are provided with target harnesses pre-installed. The final images use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7, and Hermes Agent v0.22.6.
  • Custom Dataset Pipeline: A custom dataset for agentic coding was created using the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. This pipeline combines task retrieval from existing RL environments, task generation via Repo2RLEnv, and task validation with OpenEnv.
  • Task Sources:
    • SWE-smith injects bugs into real Python and Go repositories using LLM rewrites or mutations.
    • SWE-Gym (packaged as Harbor tasks in TaskTrove) converts real GitHub issues and merged fixes into tasks.
    • Tasksmith generates tasks from merged pull requests. In one instance, Tasksmith produced 24 valid tasks from 30 merged pull requests in 10 Python repositories.

Every task in the dataset passes an eligibility screen via openenv validate and a difficulty check against the base model. Each harness adapter beat the base model under its own harness on both performance and efficiency benchmarks.

🚀 Availability

All artifacts related to this work, including adapters, GGUFs, RL tasks, and the safeagents plugin, are browsable through a Hugging Face collection. A fully reusable recipe is shared so developers can reproduce these results on their own task, harness, and model combinations.

#LLMs #ReinforcementLearning #LoRA #Agents #HuggingFace

Source: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

item.title: NVIDIA Dynamo Optimizes RL Training via Routing and Weight Updates
item.description:
NVIDIA Dynamo Optimizes RL Training via Routing and Weight Updates

NVIDIA has introduced Dynamo as a serving layer designed to address constraints in reinforcement learning (RL) training, helping teams generate more accepted training samples and complete training iterations faster. By addressing bottlenecks in rollouts, weight updates, and worker recovery, the framework aims to prevent GPU capacity waste and training delays as RL workloads scale.

🧩 How RL Training Scales

Reinforcement learning uses rewards to train models to solve problems and complete tasks. The training process relies on several key components:

  • Workers generate rollouts, which are sequences of model outputs, actions, and environment interactions.
  • RL Frameworks score the results, update model weights, and send those weights back to the workers for the next round.
  • Dynamo sits between rollout orchestration and inference workers, routing generation requests from the RL framework to eligible inference capacity.

⚙️ Key Details: Addressing Training Bottlenecks

As RL training scales, redundant compute, slow rollouts, and worker failures can delay progress. Dynamo addresses these issues through specific mechanisms:

  • Routing and Cache Reuse: Multiple RL attempts often begin with identical instructions or contexts. Dynamo’s router balances KV cache reuse and worker load, sending requests to workers that have already cached the prompt to avoid repeated processing.
  • ModelExpress Weight Updates: Sending full model checkpoints to every worker is time-consuming and can interrupt generation. ModelExpress uses delta weight transfer, sending a compressed representation of what changed rather than the full model. Compatible workers can also copy weights directly from another GPU over NIXL.
  • Recovery and Resilience: When a worker fails, Dynamo detects the loss and directs new requests toward eligible healthy workers. It adds replacement workers to the routing pool once they have loaded a checkpoint and applied subsequent deltas to catch up.

📊 Real-World Applications

Several organizations have utilized NVIDIA Dynamo and ModelExpress to optimize their RL workloads:

Organization Application
Microsoft AI Used Dynamo to support RL rollout inference during post-training.
CoreWeave Uses Dynamo and ModelExpress to accelerate model weight updates by up to 15×.
Cognition Used Dynamo to manage inference workers and route rollouts during the post-training of SWE-1.7.
Prime Intellect Uses Dynamo for distributed inference orchestration.
H Company Used Dynamo and ModelExpress to reduce average training-step time by up to 20% and GPU-hours by up to 5%.

💡 Why it matters

Addressing rollout bottlenecks allows teams to complete more training iterations within a fixed compute budget. By ensuring that GPU capacity is not wasted on redundant prefix processing or slow weight transfers, Dynamo helps maintain the momentum of the training run, even as model weights are updated and infrastructure fails.

#NVIDIA #ReinforcementLearning #Dynamo #GPUTechnology #LLMTraining

Source: Reducing Rollout Bottlenecks in Reinforcement Learning with NVIDIA Dynamo | NVIDIA Technical Blog

item.title: Residual reinforcement learning improves task completion
item.description:
Residual reinforcement learning improves task completion

Residual reinforcement learning corrects an imitation-trained base policy using a limited budget of environment interaction. This approach is particularly effective in tasks with multiple phases, where the budget must be divided among them.

🔍 Overview

  • Residual reinforcement learning improves task completion by correcting an imitation-trained base policy.
  • The method is applied to tasks with several phases, requiring the budget of environment interaction to be divided among these phases.

🧩 How it works

  • The completion gain is formalized as the change in full-task completion probability when a state-feedback controller replaces selected components of the base policy’s action during a single phase.
  • The completion gain is decomposed into the probability of reaching the phase and the conditional improvement in completion from the start of the phase.
  • Positive estimates of the completion gain determine which action components the residual policy corrects and how training episodes are distributed across phases.

⚙️ Key details

  • In stochastic point-mass docking experiments, most failures occurred in the final docking phase, but the largest completion gain occurred in the preceding channel phase.
  • Gain-based allocation improved completion over allocation proportional to failure counts and, in a variant with a longer approach, over uniform allocation at half of the budget.
  • In simulated bimanual robotic assembly, the completion-gain estimates were positive only for insertion and release, although few failures occurred during release.
  • In a second assembly configuration, a residual policy trained in the release phase improved completion from held-out states at the start of release by 16.9%.

#ResidualRL #ReinforcementLearning #Robotics #AI

Source: Improving Imitation Policies for Multi-Phase Tasks through Residual Learning Allocation

item.title: New Method Improves Vision-Language Models for Dexterous Robot Hands
item.description:
New Method Improves Vision-Language Models for Dexterous Robot Hands

🔍 Overview

Researchers have developed a method to enhance Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for dexterous robotic manipulation, addressing a key limitation: most datasets use parallel-jaw grippers, making transfer to multi-fingered hands difficult. This work explores fine-tuning strategies to adapt VLAs for dexterous hands using supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL).

🧩 How it works

The study evaluates five fine-tuning approaches with a LEAP hand and two simulation tasks, using only a few demonstrations. Key techniques include:

  • Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) paired with Diffusion-Steering Reinforcement Learning (DSRL) to adapt VLAs for dexterous manipulation.
  • Freezing the Vision-Language Model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert for better steerability.
  • Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) as a less effective approach compared to other methods.

The research identifies three critical insights:

  • SFT success does not correlate well with post-DSRL effectiveness, meaning optimal SFT checkpoints are not always the best for steering.
  • Freezing the VLM and training the action expert alone yields the most effective policy.
  • LoRA is the least steerable fine-tuning approach.

⚙️ Key details

Fine-Tuning Recipes Evaluated

Recipe Description Key Insight
Freezing VLM, tuning action expert Most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements
SFT with DSRL Insight 1: SFT success ≠ post-DSRL success
Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) Least steerable approach

Evaluation Metrics

  • Tasks: Two simulation tasks using a LEAP hand.
  • Demonstrations: Only a handful of demonstrations used.

item.description:
RadixArk Releases DaisyRose-27B Model With RL Training on Long-Horizon Agent Tasks

RadixArk has released DaisyRose-27B, its first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using the Miles framework. The model was trained on 1,200 curated long-horizon agent tasks over 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs, achieving a Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 improvement from 5.6% to 12.0%.

🔍 Overview

  • First model release from RadixArk
  • Base: Qwen3.8-27B
  • Training method: Reinforcement learning via Miles (open-source RL framework)
  • Training scale: 1,200 tasks, sessions up to 1M tokens, 18 days, 144 H200 GPUs
  • License: Apache 2.0 checkpoints available

🧩 How It Works

Task Design

  • Tasks built in partnership with Eigent AI from a large pool covering machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields
  • Thousands of candidates filtered to ~1,200 final tasks using three criteria:
    • Each task targets a mistake the original Qwen3.8-27B makes
    • Tasks redesigned around those mistakes, difficulty adjusted until solve rate falls in a useful learning range
    • Each task requires several interdependent steps: the agent must reason, plan, and execute across a long job
  • Each attempt runs up to 1.5 hours in a sandbox with >100 tool calls and >256K output tokens
  • Tasks must reward actually solving the problem; every task reviewed alongside model attempts; flawed tasks fixed or removed

Training Backend (Miles)

  • Fully asynchronous mode: agent keeps working while model learns, neither waits for the other
  • 128 H200s run inference on agent tasks; 16 H200s run the trainer
  • After each step, updated model deployed to the 128 inference GPUs
  • Internal training backend built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions (up to 1M tokens) folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization

Sandbox Service

  • Built on open-source AgentENV project (RadixArk contributes fixes)
  • Mid-September to mid-November: ~944,000 sandboxes run, up to 1,566 concurrent
  • Service scaled from 1 to 12 machines
  • 10 upgrades shipped, nearly all while training was running
  • 99% sandbox creation success across 9 weeks; >99.95% since late October

⚙️ Key Details

Benchmark Results

Benchmark Qwen3.8-27B DaisyRose-27B
Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 5.6% 12.0%

  • Gains also on reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks

Model Architecture

  • Retains Qwen3.8-27B architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window
  • Longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories

item.title: AI coding toolkit updates remove legacy DSH support and refine agent rules
item.description:
AI coding toolkit updates remove legacy DSH support and refine agent rules

The professional-grade AI coding toolkit has released an update that removes support for the legacy DeepSeek Harness (DSH) code and refines how agent instructions are managed across multiple platforms. This update introduces machine-enforced safety features, expands skill libraries, and adjusts how global and local installations interact with project-specific rules.

🔍 Overview

The toolkit now includes 116 skills and 44 agents, offering multi-platform support for tools such as Claude, Cursor, Windsurf, Copilot, Gemini, Cline, Roo Code, Aider, Augment, Antigravity, Codex CLI, and opencode. It features machine-enforced safety, lifecycle hooks, persona presets, opt-in plugin packs, and benchmark tooling. The update explicitly removes the last DeepSeek Harness (DSH) code (v5.4.0). Consequently, ai-toolkit dsh is now an unknown command, --editors dsh is an unknown editor, and the toolkit no longer migrates old DSH project skills or registry entries.

🧩 How it works

  • Security Auditing: The security-auditor reviews source code, configurations, and dependencies, then verifies fixes with local checks.
  • Agent Instructions: Project instructions reside in a committed AGENTS.md file, which CLAUDE.md imports. The ai-toolkit adopt-agents-md command moves existing CLAUDE.md content to AGENTS.md. This process ensures that nothing truncates the file, with Codex project_doc_max_bytes raised and 24,000-byte Antigravity warnings accounted for.
  • Rule Management: A toolkit-generated AGENTS.md file (marked # AI Toolkit Instructions) is no longer imported, preventing Claude from loading rules from ~/.claude/rules/ twice. The adopt-agents-md command refuses to merge into this specific file. Agents other than Claude Code do not read that file.
  • Hooks and Triggers: Hooks run from the hooks.json directory and gate only run_command. Workspace rules carry trigger frontmatter and are designed to fit Antigravity’s size limits.
  • MCP Server Integration: Injected servers, such as rag-mcp, are written to each claude-switch profile, similar to mcp install. The remove-mcp and uninstall commands clean these entries. Registered rules that require an MCP server only reach a file when its readers have that server; rag-mcp-legal-rules remains an opt-in feature.
  • Local vs. Global Installation: install --local installs everything a client can load from $HOME before project files, using the recorded global profile. The --no-global flag opts out of this, and update preserves the profile.

⚙️ Key details

  • Model Support: Skills and defaults reference Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, while the Codex reference includes GPT-6.1 Sol.
  • Language Scoping: Language knowledge skills (e.g., rust-rules, kotlin-patterns) are scoped to languages used by registered projects. After running ai-toolkit install --local in at least one project, the global install turns off other languages’ skills through skillOverrides in ~/.claude/settings.json to prevent their descriptions from loading into every session.
  • Workflow Migration: All 13 legacy workflows remain available alongside their skills. The Doctor tool checks the global global_workflows directory and provides migration instructions for specific clients.
  • Status Reporting: Redirecting account status to a legacy-encoded pipe preserves readable progress bars and paths. A refused usage read displays Unavailable: rate_limited, retry in 40m from the provider’s Retry-After header (retry_after_seconds in JSON), occurring once per account.
  • Requirements: The toolkit requires Node.js >= 18 and Python >= 3.11. It will not run on /usr/bin/python3 if it is Python 3.9.

💡 Why it matters

Claude Code automatically picks up the 116 skills, 44 agents, quality hooks, and the safety constitution. Global Claude MCP installs reach every claude-switch profile. This structure ensures that developers can maintain rigorous security standards and efficient agent behavior across a wide range of coding environments without manually managing redundant rule files or unsupported legacy commands.

item.title: verl-SpeCo adds speculative decoding to reinforcement learning loops
item.description:
verl-SpeCo adds speculative decoding to reinforcement learning loops

🧩 Overview

verl-SpeCo is a lightweight overlay for the verl reinforcement learning framework that enables the training and integration of speculative decoding drafters. It operates as an import-only dependency, keeping upstream verl unpatched while adding drafter collection, training, and hot-update logic through the verl_speco module. The tool is run via python -m verl_speco.main and composes upstream PPO/GRPO configurations. It supports multiple drafter backends—including EAGLE-1, EAGLE-2, EAGLE3, DFlash, DSpark, Domino, and P-EAGLE—along with integration for both vLLM and SGLang rollout engines.

⚙️ How It Works

The overlay performs drafter co-training directly within the reinforcement learning loop. It collects hidden states during rollout or old-logprob computation, periodically trains the drafter, and publishes the updated weights back to the rollout engine. A key mechanism, known as “Bubble Time” training, utilizes rollout idle workers to run drafter optimizer steps. This approach publishes the trained drafter to all replicas, preserving generation benefits while keeping the drafter training time off the main critical path.

The tool maintains architectural flexibility; the drafter trainer runs on FSDP2, while the main actor can utilize verl’s FSDP/FSDP2 or VeOmni model engine.

📊 Performance Metrics

The overlay exposes step-level observability, including drafter timing and vLLM speculative decoding acceptance metrics such as drafter/spec_decode/mean_acceptance_length. Recent results cover both NPU EAGLE3 co-training and GPU DFlash Bubble Time training.

  • Qwen3-8B on vLLM-Ascend/NPU: Using an EAGLE3 drafter for 100 steps, co-training increased mean acceptance length compared to a fixed-drafter setup. Relative to the baseline, this yielded approximately 20% faster rollout and 11% faster end-to-end training without accuracy regression.
  • Qwen3-4B GPU run: In a DFlash run utilizing Bubble Time, the drafter training quota remained aligned with the synchronous path while shifting most drafter work off the main critical path. Excluding checkpoint-save steps, the end-to-end step time improved by about 6.7% compared with synchronous training, with similar acceptance length.

🛠️ Backend and Runtime Details

Specific configurations govern how different backends operate. EAGLE-1 and EAGLE-2 share vLLM’s native draft method, with EAGLE-2 adding a dynamic-tree decoding policy. Domino is trained using the DOMINO speculative algorithm but served as a DFlash projector sub-mode.

When serving a Domino checkpoint for rollout, speculative_algorithm=DFLASH must be used on an engine version supporting the Domino projector. Additionally, LK loss is not supported for Domino; dflash_lk_loss_alpha and dspark_lk_loss_alpha must be set to zero, as positive values are rejected during layout resolution. While P-EAGLE training is available, its vLLM parallel-drafting rollout runtime is not yet integrated into the overlay, requiring users to keep rollout drafter serving disabled and manage training or serving separately. Standalone smoke tests for GPU training are maintained under tests/special_standalone/ and can be executed via scheduled or manual workflows.

item.title: Are Dense Rewards Worth Their Tokens in GRPO?
item.description:
Are Dense Rewards Worth Their Tokens in GRPO?

Recent work on reinforcement learning from human feedback examines whether dense rewards are worth their tokens in group-relative policy optimization (GRPO).

🔍 Overview

Reinforcement learning from human feedback trains language models to reason by rewarding correct final answers. A widely used algorithm, group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), gives every token of a solution the same credit. Because of this, dense process rewards have been proposed to credit intermediate steps, for example with a Monte-Carlo reward that scores each step by sampling continuations from it.

🧩 How it works

Comparing such a reward with GRPO per training update, or vetting it with a gradient test on a single batch, leaves out what it costs: in the setting, the continuations alone take 91% of all generated tokens.

The work introduces a matched-compute protocol that gives every training intervention the same budget, measured in generated tokens and training GPU-hours, and tests it in preregistered studies with controls for side effects.

⚙️ Key details

  • Across 1,668 runs on six models, matching compute reverses the ranking.
  • On Qwen2.5-1.5B, the Monte-Carlo reward leads standard GRPO per update, yet ends 14.3 percentage points lower at equal tokens and 7.8 points lower at equal training time, and none of four dense-reward variants outperforms GRPO even with as much training time.
  • A per-token gradient test orders these rewards as training does but overestimates each by one to two points, as much as the gains it is meant to detect.
  • In contrast, training on the prompts whose predicted success is nearest 1/2 improves accuracy at matched compute, by 1.7 points on Qwen3-0.6B and 0.8 on Qwen2.5-1.5B.
  • The gains replicate on fresh seeds and unseen problems, and a simple rule, that the candidate prompts are predicted to fail more often than not, predicted where they appear in five of six preregistered tests.
  • Both gains come early in training, and standard GRPO with twice the initial learning rate comes within half a point of them.
  • The study argues that training interventions should be validated at matched compute, which overturns some apparent gains and confirms others.

💡 Why it matters

  • The study reports that matching compute reverses the ranking.
  • It also reports that standard GRPO with twice the initial learning rate comes within half a point of the gains from training on prompts predicted to fail more often than not.
  • The evidence therefore presents a caution about evaluating dense rewards without matched compute.

#GRPO #ReinforcementLearning #DenseRewards

Source: Exploration via Exploitation: The Blessing of Reward Diversity in Personalized Federated RL Source: Branch-and-Commit for Frozen RL Agents: When and Where to Spend Test-Time Compute Source: FaST: Factored Synthesis of Transitions for Offline Reinforcement Learning Source: Making Strides in Symbolic Imitation Learning: Offline Demonstrations, Online Tuning Source: Audited Gradients, Anchored Policies: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning for Efficient Flow Control Source: Are Dense Rewards Worth Their Tokens in GRPO?

NVIDIA Alpamayo 2 Edge Brings Adaptive Reasoning to On‑Board Autonomous Driving

🔍 Overview

  • It is paired with a diffusion action expert to turn surround‑camera observations, temporal context, and navigation inputs into Chain‑of‑Causation (CoC) reasoning traces and future driving trajectories.
  • The model is built for edge deployment, preserving reasoning quality while fitting the inference budget of an onboard stack.

Nemotron 2 B backbone (Cosmos 3 Edge) Core reasoning engine

  • Adaptive reasoning reduces unnecessary token generation, conserving inference compute during routine driving.
  • Multi‑resolution inputs encode surround‑view observations online.

  • Offline distillation uses CoC reasoning autolabels generated by Alpamayo 2 Super.

  • Zero‑shot evaluation showed a 13.6 % reduction in displacement error (minADE) and a 46.1 % reduction in lateral prediction error (RMSE at 3 s) compared to Alpamayo 2 Super, despite sensor differences.
  • Fine‑tuning on proprietary driving data delivered an additional 44.2 % reduction in displacement error versus the Alpamayo 2 Edge baseline.
  • Within 48 hours, Alpamayo 2 Edge ran at 10 Hz on AGX Thor for real‑time planning.

item.title: FlexFloor Enables Faster Reinforcement Learning Post‑Training for Large Language Models
item.description:
FlexFloor Enables Faster Reinforcement Learning Post‑Training for Large Language Models

FlexFloor is a system that reduces the compute bottleneck of reinforcement‑learning (RL) post‑training for large language models by releasing resources earlier during synchronous response generation.

🔍 Overview

  • RL post‑training improves the capabilities of large language models, but generating training responses consumes most of the compute.
  • In mixture‑of‑experts models, workers that finish generating their assigned responses often stay occupied because their experts are still needed by other workers processing longer responses.
  • About one‑third of occupied worker time in the baseline occurs after the local response generation has already finished.

🧩 How it works

  • FlexFloor jointly adapts response scheduling and the active group of workers.
  • It leverages historical response lengths and memory constraints to decide how to batch prompts and where to place them.
  • Workers are progressively released once their expert computation is no longer required, while preserving expert availability and correct inter‑worker communication.

📈 Results

Metric Improvement compared to baseline
Response tokens per occupied computing time +65.40%
Throughput (responses generated per unit time) +52.74%
Rollout reward variation Little observed change
  • FlexFloor generates roughly 65 % more response tokens for the same amount of occupied compute time.
  • Overall response generation throughput rises by about 53 %.
  • These gains are achieved without noticeable degradation in RL rollout reward.

💡 Why it matters

  • By making RL post‑training more compute‑efficient, FlexFloor shortens the development cycle for large language models and AI agents.
  • Faster, cheaper iteration enables more frequent updates and experimentation, supporting ongoing improvements in model performance.
  • The approach maintains correctness of expert communication, ensuring that efficiency gains do not compromise training quality.

#ReinforcementLearning #LLM #ResourceEfficiency #AITraining

item.title: Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation Improves Knowledge Transfer from Large Models
item.description:
Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation Improves Knowledge Transfer from Large Models

From Solver Trajectories to Teaching Trajectories: Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation was submitted on 27 Oct 2026 to the Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence category. The paper introduces a new approach to knowledge distillation from large reasoning models (LRMs).

🔍 Overview

  • Traditional distillation often uses raw teacher trajectories as supervision.
  • This creates a mismatch because advanced LRMs are optimized as strong solvers via reward‑driven post‑training (e.g., RLHF), not as teachers that produce reasoning processes smaller models can easily learn.
  • Smaller models have different “cognitive capacities” than their larger teachers, so directly imitating raw trajectories can be ineffective and typically needs many high‑quality samples.

🧩 How it works

  • The authors propose Cognition‑Aligned Reasoning Distillation (CARD), an RL‑based framework that transforms existing solver trajectories into teaching trajectories aligned with the student’s cognition.
  • CARD avoids expensive resampling by directly converting the original trajectories.
  • Optimization relies on two reward signals:
    1. Distribution Alignment Reward – matches the student’s predictive distribution.
    2. Logical Coherence Reward – reduces misleading failed reasoning steps.

⚙️ Key details

  • CARD is evaluated across multiple student models and settings.
  • Results show CARD outperforms distillation from raw teacher trajectories in in‑domain settings.
  • CARD also achieves substantial gains in out‑of‑distribution performance.

🚀 Availability

  • The code for CARD is released at the provided https URL.

💡 Why it matters

  • By aligning teacher trajectories with the student’s cognition, CARD addresses the mismatch between solver‑focused training of LRMs and the learning needs of smaller models, reducing the need for large numbers of high‑quality teacher samples.

#knowledge-distillation #large-models #reinforcement-learning

Source: From Solver Trajectories to Teaching Trajectories: Cognition-Aligned Reasoning Distillation

item.title: CONCUR Introduces Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi‑Task RL
item.description:
CONCUR Introduces Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi‑Task RL

When a Large Language Model (LLM) is trained with Reinforcement Learning (RL) on multiple tasks, the primary reward can gate auxiliary rewards such as a length reward. Existing group‑relative advantage estimators may treat a gated auxiliary like any other component, which can reverse the primary’s ordering and allow auxiliaries to dominate at the primary’s ceiling. Keeping gated auxiliaries harms some tasks, while dropping them harms others.

🔍 Overview

  • Paper title: CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi‑Task, Multi‑Reward Reinforcement Learning
  • Submitted to Computer Science > Computation and Language on 27 Oct 2026.
  • Goal: Align auxiliary rewards with the primary reward so that they never contradict the primary ordering.

🧩 How it works

  • CONCUR replaces each gated auxiliary’s standardized score with the nearest score that satisfies two conditions:
    1. Responses with higher primary rewards cannot receive lower scores.
    2. Responses that have reached the primary’s ceiling receive equal scores.
  • Two variants are defined:
    • CONCUR‑T – enforces both conditions continuously throughout training.
    • CONCUR‑A – relaxes the second condition for an auxiliary when it agrees with the primary’s order more often than it reverses it among passing responses.

⚙️ Variants & Features

  • CONCUR‑T: strict monotonicity and ceiling equality.
  • CONCUR‑A: conditional lifting of the ceiling‑equality rule based on agreement frequency.
  • Applies to any gated auxiliary reward in multi‑task RL settings.

📈 Results

  • Evaluated on three models from two families across four task types:
    • Mathematics
    • Code generation
    • Instruction following
    • Writing
  • Both CONCUR‑T and CONCUR‑A achieve higher average scores than all baselines and higher than the configuration where all gated auxiliaries are dropped.

💡 Why it matters

  • Provides a systematic way to keep auxiliary rewards concordant with the primary objective, improving performance across diverse downstream tasks without sacrificing any specific task.

#ReinforcementLearning #MultiTaskLearning #LanguageModels #AIResearch

Source: CONCUR: Concordant Auxiliary Rewards for Multi-Task, Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning

item.title: Amazon SageMaker AI Introduces Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning for Agents
item.description:
Amazon SageMaker AI Introduces Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning for Agents

Amazon SageMaker AI has introduced Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning (MTRL), a serverless capability designed to train models on sequences of actions where the only reliable feedback is whether the entire sequence succeeded.

💡 Why it matters

Most fine-tuning focuses on producing a better answer to a single prompt. However, agents performing tasks like triaging support tickets or filing expense reports require a sequence of actions where each step depends on previous outcomes. Traditional supervised fine-tuning lacks labels for these sequences, and single-turn reinforcement learning cannot credit decisions made several steps before an outcome.

🧩 How it works

Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning trains models using the following architecture and process:

  • Infrastructure: SageMaker AI owns the training job and policy model. It sends prompts through an AWS Lambda forwarder to an agent hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore or other infrastructure such as Amazon EKS, Amazon EC2, or AWS Fargate.
  • Execution: The agent calls the policy model, acts in the environment for as many turns as needed, and reports a single reward at the end of the episode.
  • Optimization: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) updates a Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapter on the policy model based on the spread of rewards across several rollouts of the same word.
  • Deployment: A single Python file deployed to AgentCore contains the environment, the tool, and the scoring function.

⚙️ Key details

To demonstrate MTRL, a run was conducted using the game Wordle and the GPT-OSS-20B model. Wordle was selected because its rules are few, guesses depend on previous feedback, and outcomes are scored objectively.

Metric Result

Solve rate (default reasoning) Increased from 61% to 84%
Solve rate (low effort) Increased from 15% to 69%
Training cost Approximately $339 in training tokens
Training duration 12 hours 40 minutes
Total rollouts 105,486

Training Token Consumption:

  • Prefill: 491.6 million
  • Sample: 159.7 million
  • Train: 643.3 million

🚀 Availability

  • Privacy: Datasets, agents, and trained models remain in the user’s AWS account and are not used to train base models.
  • Code: All code is available in the accompanying aws-samples repository.
  • Billing: The AgentCore runtime is billed separately for vCPU and memory usage.

item.title: Amazon SageMaker AI adds serverless training session APIs for custom model fine‑tuning
item.description:
Amazon SageMaker AI adds serverless training session APIs for custom model fine‑tuning

🔍 Overview

Amazon SageMaker AI has expanded its serverless model‑customization offering with the general‑availability launch of training sessions. The new APIs let customers write and coordinate their own post‑training logic—such as custom loss functions or reward signals—while SageMaker AI handles all GPU infrastructure, fault recovery, and checkpoint storage.

🧩 How it works

Training sessions expose low‑level operations (e.g., forward_backward(), optim_step(), sample()) as SageMaker API calls. Users write the training loop in their own Python process; each call is executed on a live, stateful GPU‑backed session. The service takes care of:

  • GPU allocation and distributed execution
  • Gradient synchronization and checkpoint storage
  • Fault recovery, tenant isolation, and scaling
  • Security configuration via IAM roles, optional KMS keys, and VPC settings

Your data, checkpoints, and any custom weights stay in your Amazon S3 bucket in the region you choose, and SageMaker does not reuse them to train other models.

⚙️ Key Features

  • No instance‑type or cluster management – the service automatically provisions serverless GPUs.
  • Fine‑grained algorithmic control – write custom loss, reward, or preference functions.
  • Multi‑turn reinforcement learning – managed, serverless support for agents that require several interaction rounds.
  • Flexible adaptation – choose Low‑Rank Adaptation (LoRA) or full fine‑tuning, and chain techniques through continuous customization.
  • Pay‑per‑token pricing model.
  • Secure execution – IAM execution role, optional KMS key, VPC configuration, data stays in your S3 bucket.
  • Evaluation before deployment – built‑in steps for accuracy, bias, and safety checks.

📚 Programming Model

Training sessions are accessed through three SageMaker Python SDK clients:

  1. ServiceClient – sets platform‑level settings (execution role, model package, S3 output location, optional KMS/VPC) and starts a session.
  2. TrainingClient – provides operations such as forward(), forward_backward(), optim_step(), and checkpoint handling.
  3. SamplingClient – handles sample() and compute_logprobs() for generation and scoring during roll‑outs.

Each API call maps to a single step in your loop. An active session also exposes an OpenAI‑compatible chat completions endpoint, enabling existing client code to sample from the customized model.

🚀 Availability

The training‑session APIs are now generally available as part of SageMaker AI serverless model customization. A companion training sessions cookbook provides ready‑to‑run SFT and RL recipes.

💡 Why it matters

Customizing an open‑weight model with post‑training techniques such as reinforcement learning or preference optimization yields more accurate results for a specific business context (e.g., product catalogs, clinical vocabularies) and reduces inference cost. The new serverless APIs remove the operational burden of managing GPU clusters, allowing teams to focus on algorithmic innovation while still retaining full control over the training procedure.

item.title: NVIDIA RTX Spark and Isaac Lab Enable Simulated Navigation Training for Microduck Robot
item.description:
NVIDIA RTX Spark and Isaac Lab Enable Simulated Navigation Training for Microduck Robot

NVIDIA demonstrated an end‑to‑end workflow that uses RTX Spark, Isaac Lab, and Omniverse tools to create a simulated obstacle course, train a navigation policy for the Microduck robot, and evaluate the policy in Isaac Sim.

🔍 Overview

  • Teaching a robot to navigate an obstacle course requires perception, balance, and the ability to adjust actions when obstacles block the path ahead, not just a walking policy.
  • The development process links three stages: creating assets and an environment, using physics simulation to model robot‑environment interaction, and training + evaluating policies in simulation.

🛠️ Tools and Roles

Component Role
RTX Spark Local development hub; supports AI‑assisted planning, policy validation, and receives trained policies for local evaluation in Isaac Sim.
Isaac Lab Cloud‑based robot‑learning framework for reinforcement learning.
Newton Models physical behavior for simulation.
Omniverse libraries Generate simulated visual observations via RTX rendering.
Isaac Sim Runs local evaluation of trained policies returned from RTX Spark.
Hermes Translates prompts into step‑by‑step project plans and creates asset inventories from images.
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt Works with Hermes to generate project plans and analyze images for reusable assets.
Astra Builds and tests assets; directs FreeCAD geometry creation and Blender material application.
SimReady Central Library Free, ungated library of >2,000 simulation‑ready OpenUSD assets.
Microduck Reference quadruped robot used for navigation training.

📐 Workflow Steps

  1. Write a natural‑language prompt that describes the obstacle course and what Microduck must learn.
  2. On RTX Spark, Hermes and NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Bolt translate the prompt into a detailed project plan (task, resources, outputs, stages).
  3. Review official Microduck documentation and summarize its capabilities, constraints, and unknowns.
  4. Define the course layout, obstacle dimensions, clearances, and intended route.
  5. Generate a photorealistic concept image using a verified Microduck reference image.
  6. Hermes and Nemotron analyze the concept image, extract unique reusable assets, assign identifiers, and create cropped reference images.
  7. Astra enhances the references, models geometry in FreeCAD, and adds fine details and materials in Blender.
  8. Assemble the assets into a simulated environment; Newton provides physics, Omniverse renders visuals.
  9. Train a navigation policy with Isaac Lab in the cloud using the simulated environment.
  10. Return the trained policy to RTX Spark and evaluate it locally in Isaac Sim.
  11. Verify robot capabilities, test navigation, obstacle handling, and reset logic—all in simulation (no physical hardware).
  12. Package the plan, robot brief, concept, asset inventory, crops, and execution instructions for reproducibility.

📊 What You’ll Learn

  • How to create a simulated obstacle course for a quadruped robot.
  • How AI agents (Hermes, Nemotron, Astra) automate planning, asset extraction, and 3D modeling.
  • How to train a navigation policy with Isaac Lab and validate it with RTX Spark and Isaac Sim.
  • How to leverage the SimReady Central Library for reusable simulation assets.

item.title: Study Finds Filtering Old SEC News Boosts LLM‑Based Portfolio Returns
item.description:
Study Finds Filtering Old SEC News Boosts LLM‑Based Portfolio Returns

Financial news continues to affect investment decisions even after it is published. A new analysis compares how reinforcement‑learning (RL) policies and a large language model (LLM) handle aging news when building portfolios.

🔍 Overview

  • Financial news can influence decisions long after publication.
  • Timely news may reach investors before prices fully adjust; older news may already be reflected in prices.
  • The study evaluates two approaches to aging signals: keep the signals and give timing information to a portfolio policy, or filter the signals out before selection.

🧩 How it works

  • A fixed LLM extracts signals from public SEC disclosures.
  • These signals are fed either to RL policies or directly to the LLM, which then chooses portfolios.
  • Historical tests covering 2023‑2025 include trading‑cost adjustments.

📊 Results

  • RL policies: In a controlled test, RL choices responded to timing information, but historical returns showed no consistent benefit from adding timing data.
  • LLM‑based selection: Filtering out old news produced the highest average net return, 18.43 % per year when news delivery was delayed by four weeks.
  • The LLM’s filtered‑news return exceeded the returns of all RL strategies that used news.

📈 Why it matters

  • Filtering aging news can improve net returns for LLM‑driven portfolio allocation.
  • The result suggests that, for this data set, older news may add noise rather than value when included in RL‑based strategies.

item.title: Microsoft Research Asia releases Harnessed Agentic RL with Agent Lightning v1.0
item.description:
Microsoft Research Asia releases Harnessed Agentic RL with Agent Lightning v1.0

Microsoft Research Asia introduced the Harnessed Agentic RL training paradigm and open‑sourced Agent Lightning v1.0, a lightweight framework that lets the same agent harness used in deployment participate directly in reinforcement learning.

🔍 Overview

  • Harnessed Agentic RL removes the need to reimplement the agent inside the training framework.
  • Agent Lightning v1.0 provides a complete agent RL control plane in roughly 3,500 lines of code.
  • The framework runs agents as standard Kubernetes jobs on self‑managed clusters, cloud Kubernetes, or local infrastructure, without reliance on paid commercial sandbox services.

🧩 How it works

  • The agent continues to call the model through an LLM proxy; the training system only observes the request‑response pairs.
  • The agent harness that coordinates the deployed agent also handles the environment interaction loop during training.
  • Because only LLM calls are recorded, a single rollout can be split into a variable number of training samples.
  • Retokenization is required to obtain token IDs; re‑tokenizing text can shift token boundaries, so adjacent calls may not be merged into one sample.

⚙️ Key details

  • Lightweight design – the entire codebase is about 3,500 lines, making it easy to understand, modify, and extend.
  • Native Kubernetes support – agents run directly as Kubernetes jobs, supporting self‑managed, cloud, and local clusters.
  • Data‑efficient training recipe – an end‑to‑end coding‑agent pipeline raised Qwen3.5‑9B from 41.8 % to 56.4 % Pass@1 on SWE‑bench Verified, a 14.6 percentage‑point gain using only ≈6,000 training samples from an open‑sourced dataset.
  • Traditional vs. harnessed RL – conventional agentic RL assumes the training framework owns the interaction loop, requiring developers to rebuild the agent’s context management, tool protocols, and execution logic inside the RL framework. This rebuilding is costly and can produce a training agent that differs from the deployed agent.

📊 Early systems and agents

💡 Why it matters

  • AI agents now consist of complex full‑stack systems; their capabilities increasingly depend on the agent harness that coordinates them from outside the model.
  • Harnessed Agentic RL aligns the training environment with the deployment environment, eliminating the mismatch that arises when agents are rebuilt for training.

item.description:
Amazon SageMaker AI MTRL Enables Multi‑Turn RL Fine‑Tuning of LLMs

Amazon SageMaker AI MTRL lets you fine‑tune large language models with reinforcement learning in multi‑turn interaction settings.

🔍 Overview

  • Fine‑tunes LLMs using reinforcement learning in multi‑turn interaction settings.
  • Demonstrated by fine‑tuning a Qwen3.6‑27B model (supported in the US West (Oregon) Region us‑west‑2) for a search agent.

🛠️ How it works

  • Frames an agentic task as a sequence of decisions.
  • Generates training data through multi‑turn rollouts.
  • Optimizes the model with policy‑gradient algorithms.
  • Supports algorithms such as Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Clipped Important Sampling Policy Optimization (CISPO), and importance‑sampling (IS) losses, paired with group‑based advantage estimators (GRPO, GRPO pass@k, RLOO, and more).

  • Modular agent‑environment interface – low‑code integration.
  • Serverless execution – production‑scale agentic RL at per‑token pricing without provisioning or managing GPU clusters.
  • Asynchronous rollout & trajectory collection – parallel generation and gradient updates.
  • Native algorithm library – PPO, CISPO, IS losses with GRPO, GRPO pass@k, RLOO, etc.
  • Resumable training – continue beyond single‑job time limits.
  • Trajectory and reward observability – inspect agent actions turn by turn via MLflow managed by Amazon SageMaker AI.

item.title: Accelerating Mixture-of-Experts Training with Amazon EKS, EFA, and DeepEP
item.description:
Accelerating Mixture-of-Experts Training with Amazon EKS, EFA, and DeepEP

AWS has described an architecture optimized to accelerate the training of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, specifically addressing the infrastructure challenges associated with large-scale Reinforcement Learning (RL) post-training.

🔍 Overview

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a standard architecture for scaling large language models (LLMs) to hundreds of billions or trillions of parameters while maintaining efficient inference through sparsity. However, large-scale RL training—including pipelines based on Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)—places unusual demands on infrastructure. These demands arise because RL combines elastic inference work with tightly coupled model training that requires high-bandwidth communication.

⚙️ Key Details

Large-scale asynchronous RL jobs must optimize two distinct, simultaneous workloads:

  • Rollout Generation: Distributed inference focused on maximizing aggregate throughput rather than minimizing inter-token latency or time to first token (TTFT).
  • Policy Training: Tightly coupled workers that progress in lockstep; any straggling worker or latency spike can trigger NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) timeouts or stall the entire job.

Training MoE models introduces specific constraints compared to dense models. As architectures become more sparse to reduce inference costs, training is constrained more by communication than by compute. A primary source of this overhead is Expert Parallelism (EP), which introduces dynamic all-to-all token routing across devices in addition to standard Tensor Parallelism (TP), Data Parallelism (DP), and Pipeline Parallelism (PP).

🧩 How it works

To address these challenges, an architecture combining the following tools is used:

Component Purpose
Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) Orchestrates large-scale RL training and coordinates heterogeneous compute.
Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) Accelerates large-scale RL training and provides high-bandwidth inter-node communication.
DeepEP Optimizes expert-parallel communication over EFA.

This system must balance three resource constraints to prevent bottlenecks or idle capacity:

  • Accelerator compute
  • Memory (including KV-cache capacity for distributed inference)
  • Network bandwidth

item.title: Introduction of Pistis Multimodal Model Family and New RL Frameworks
item.description:
Introduction of Pistis Multimodal Model Family and New RL Frameworks

Recent developments in multimodal large language models have led to the introduction of the Pistis model family and several new reinforcement learning (RL) optimization frameworks designed to improve reasoning, reduce hallucinations, and enhance agentic performance.

🔍 Overview

The Pistis model family consists of multimodal large language models built on Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6. These models are developed using a scalable post-training framework that begins with large-scale multimodal supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

Model Variant Base Architecture Primary Purpose
Pistis-9B Qwen3.5 General multimodal capabilities
Pistis-27B Qwen3.6 General multimodal capabilities
Pistis-Thinking Varies Strengthening deep multimodal reasoning
Pistis-Agentic Varies Long-horizon planning, iterative reasoning, and tool use

🧩 How it Works

To improve these models, several novel training paradigms and systems have been introduced:

  • Interleaved Distillation and Reinforcement Learning (IDRL): A paradigm that integrates on-policy distillation and reinforcement learning in a single loop. By alternating between objectives, it aims for more effective knowledge transfer and precise credit assignment for agentic trajectories.
  • Dual-Entropy Enhanced Policy Optimization (DEEPO): This dual-stage enhancement combines signal variance regularization and gradient preconditioning to reduce hallucinations while preserving accuracy.
  • Pistis-Auto-Harnessing (PAH): A system-level method that iteratively optimizes the agent’s inference harness without updating model parameters or increasing the interaction budget.
  • Graph-based Faithful sTep-level credit-assignment (GRAFT): A framework that grafts rollout trajectories into a graph to recover node state-values via Bellman iteration, reducing bias in step-level advantage estimation.
  • SLCA-GRPO: A framework using Segment-Locked Credit Assignment to decouple advantage estimation at the structural segment level, preventing gradient noise from summary generation from leaking into tool-decision tokens.

⚙️ Key Details

Researchers have also explored RLVR (Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards) and other specific algorithmic tasks:

  • Small Model RLVR: Testing on Qwen3.5-0.8B showed a 3.8-fold gain in average exact match (0.352 vs 0.092) using a reason-over-search recipe with Wikipedia-search tools, though sparse exact-match rewards were found to be ineffective for models of this size.
  • MI-SARSA: An on-policy temporal-difference algorithm incorporating mutual-information regularization. It produces a reward-complexity tradeoff where stronger penalties lead to simpler policies and faster reaction times.
  • Optimization Landscape: Study of RLVR on algorithmic tasks suggests the landscape is benign with no local minima for certain models, meaning difficulties stem from diffusive barriers and gradient-estimation error rather than a rugged landscape.

item.title: New Evaluation Protocol and Method for Long-Horizon Reinforcement Learning Agents
item.description:
New Evaluation Protocol and Method for Long-Horizon Reinforcement Learning Agents

Researchers have introduced a new evaluation protocol called checkpoint handoff and a training method called Reward Stimulation Implicit Q-Learning (RSIQL) to improve and analyze language-model agents acting in live environments.

🔍 Overview

Reinforcement learning (RL) now trains agents capable of acting over dozens of steps in live environments. Because an agent in a closed loop writes its own inputs, the states it encounters late in an episode are partly of its own making. This creates a challenge when comparing Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) checkpoints and RL checkpoints, as they are scored from different states even on identical tasks.

🧩 How it works

To separate the factors contributing to endpoint success, the checkpoint handoff protocol clones a state reached by one released checkpoint and hands it to another without retraining. This splits endpoint gains into two metrics:

  • REACH: How often a policy arrives at a state the environment confirms is a fixed number of actions from success.
  • SOLVE: How often a policy finishes from an identical cloned state.

⚙️ Key details

Regarding the RSIQL method for offline settings with sparse rewards and long-horizon dependencies:

  • Purpose: It addresses issues where goal-completion information is temporally distant from early decisions and offline value estimation introduces error.
  • Mechanism: It uses an auxiliary goal-conditioned value function to identify intermediate states that make progress toward the goal, applying reward stimulation for less-delayed training supervision.
  • Structure: Unlike hierarchical methods, RSIQL is a simple non-hierarchical method that does not learn a separate high-level subgoal policy.

💡 Why it matters

Evaluation and experimental results show:

  • The interaction between the reacher and solver is positive across two benchmarks and two independently released pipelines.
  • On ALFWorld, RL improves both REACH and SOLVE terms, and the SFT solver never succeeds where the RL solver fails.
  • An RL history is worth more to an RL solver than the same history is to an SFT solver.
  • RSIQL improves over goal-conditioned IQL on average and achieves performance competitive with hierarchical offline goal-conditioned methods on OGBench and D4RL goal-reaching benchmarks.

#ReinforcementLearning #AIagents #MachineLearning #RSIQL

Source: Reach or Solve? Attributing Agentic RL Gains with Checkpoint Handoffs Source: Improving Offline Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning via Selective Reward Stimulation

item.title: PIVOT Enhances Vision-Language Reasoning via Experience Replay and Vision-Guided Advantage
item.description:
PIVOT Enhances Vision-Language Reasoning via Experience Replay and Vision-Guided Advantage

A new dual-level learning framework called PIVOT has been introduced to improve the reasoning capabilities of large vision‑language models by addressing key limitations of standard on‑policy RLVR algorithms.

🔍 Overview

  • Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has significantly improved the reasoning capabilities of large vision‑language models (LVLMs).
  • Standard on‑policy RLVR algorithms discard valuable visually‑grounded reasoning trajectories after a single update and allocate token advantages uniformly, which hinders reinforcement of critical perception or reasoning steps.

🧩 How it works

PIVOT anchors policy optimization around informative visual reasoning signals through two mechanisms:

  1. Self‑calibrated experience replay – selectively collects and replays historically successful visually‑grounded experiences, providing stable reference anchors for policy updates.
  2. Vision‑guided advantage allocation – adds extra vision‑aware advantages to tokens based on their local visual support and impact on downstream reasoning.

⚙️ Key details

  • Dual‑level framework combines experience replay with vision‑aware advantage shaping.
  • Replay mechanism focuses on trajectories that demonstrate strong visual grounding.
  • Advantage allocation targets tokens that are directly supported by visual context.
  • Experiments on diverse benchmarks show PIVOT achieves highly competitive performance in enhancing multimodal reasoning of LVLMs.

💡 Why it matters

  • Preserves and reinforces valuable visual reasoning trajectories instead of discarding them.
  • Enables the model to prioritize critical perception and reasoning steps during training.
  • Improves the overall multimodal reasoning capability of large vision‑language models.

item.description:
Introducing T1: A 122B Mixture-of-Experts Model for Long-Horizon Terminal Tasks

As AI agent usage shifts toward long-horizon tasks such as coding and scientific discovery, terminal tasks have become especially important. To address this, researchers have introduced T1, a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model of 122B total trained with reinforcement learning. Built to operate a real shell in a cloud sandbox for up to 300+ tool-call turns per task, the model is rewarded by executing each task’s own verifier, marking a major update in long-horizon agent capabilities.

🔍 Overview

The T1 model is designed to tackle complex terminal tasks. Unlike standard agents, T1 runs directly inside a cloud sandbox shell and uses a unique reinforcement learning pipeline to maximize the number of passing verifiers per task.

🧩 How it works

The training recipe for T1 relies on three key pillars:

  • Warm-Started Actor-Critic Training: The pipeline is aggressively warm-started to stabilize actor-critic training, using a dense process reward that scores trajectories by the absolute number of passing verifiers.
  • Stable Optimization via TITO and R3:
    • TITO Construction: The model is trained on the exact sampled token identifiers with drift repair at turn boundaries.
    • Rollout Routing Replay (R3): The pipeline records the sampler’s per-token expert choices at every MoE layer and replays them during training.
    • Combined Impact: Together, TITO and R3 cut the training-to-inference log-probability difference from 0.021 to 0.013, yielding exactly aligned zero token drift in the loss region.
  • Out-of-Distribution Training Corpus: The use of isolated seeds and synthesized tasks disjoint from Terminal-Bench 2.1 ensures that performance gains reflect genuine capability transfer rather than benchmark overfitting.

📊 Benchmark Results

The post-training pipeline significantly improves terminal task execution, outperforming established baselines.
